#Unit 2 — Idea Generation and Market Research

Lecture hours 10
Marks carried in model question 29 — two 2-markers (A3 creative thinking techniques, A4 target market), three 5-markers (B12 market needs, B13 competitor analysis, B14 trend analysis), plus case sub-parts (a) idea generation steps and (b) market analysis
Difficulty ★★★☆☆ — concepts are standard; the marks are in structure and Nepal examples. Students treat this as "common sense" and write vague answers.
Exam yield 🔴 highest in the paper — owns the case + five direct questions
Prerequisite Unit 1 (opportunity recognition → idea generation)
Syllabus bullets Techniques for Creative Thinking · Market Needs Identification · Evaluating Business Ideas · Current Technology Trend Analysis · Prototyping Development · Defining Target Markets · Competitor Analysis Tools · Consumer Behavior Insight · Case Study: Pathao Nepal

Read this first: this unit carries 29 marks (29% of the paper) including the first two case sub-parts. The questions are straightforward but demand structured answers with Nepal examples. A3 and A4 are 2-markers — write ~55 words each. B12, B13, B14 are 5-markers — write ~200 words each with framework + Nepal example. The case (D22a, D22b) uses this unit's frameworks directly.

#2.1 Techniques for creative thinking (A3)

Creative thinking techniques are structured methods to generate novel ideas — they move you from "waiting for inspiration" to "producing options on demand."

#Four examinable techniques (pick any two for A3)

Technique How it works When to use
Brainstorming group, deferred judgement, quantity → quality, build on others early divergence, team setting
SCAMPER Substitute, Combine, Adapt, Modify, Put to another use, Eliminate, Reverse — apply to existing product/service improving or pivoting an existing idea
Mind Mapping central problem → branches (who, what, where, how, why) → sub-branches solo exploration, visual thinkers
Trend Analysis scan tech/market/social trends → ask "what if this continues?" / "what is the opposite?" spotting new opportunities (links to B14)

#A3 · "List any two techniques for creative thinking." [2]

Two techniques: (1) Brainstorming — group session with deferred judgement, aim for quantity first, then build on others' ideas; best for early divergence. (2) SCAMPER — apply seven prompts (Substitute, Combine, Adapt, Modify, Put to another use, Eliminate, Reverse) to an existing product or service to generate variants; best for improving or pivoting.

(54 words. Two names + one-line how-it-works + when-to-use each.)

#2.2 Market needs identification (B12)

Market needs identification is the systematic process of discovering what target users truly need — not what they say they want — and validating that the need is urgent, pervasive, and worth paying for.

#The process (four steps for B12)

Step What you do Tools
1. Observe watch users in context; note workarounds, complaints, "hacks" contextual inquiry, shadowing, forum/social listening
2. Interview open-ended questions about problems, not solutions "Tell me about the last time you..." / "What is the hardest part of...?"
3. Quantify estimate how many have the need, how often, how much they'd pay surveys, keyword search volume, market reports
4. Validate build a minimum test (landing page, demo, concierge MVP) smoke test, pre-sell, letter of intent

#B12 · "How do you identify market needs for a new IT idea?" [5]

Shape: four-step process + one Nepal example per step. ~200 words.

Identifying market needs follows four steps:

  1. Observe — watch users in context; note workarounds, complaints, "hacks". Nepal example: observe Kathmandu commuters queuing for microbuses, using multiple apps, asking drivers for cash discounts.
  2. Interview — open-ended questions about problems, not solutions ("Tell me about the last time you..." / "What is the hardest part of...?"). Nepal example: interview 20 riders about peak-hour pain points — surge pricing, safety, driver cancellation.
  3. Quantify — estimate how many have the need, how often, how much they'd pay. Nepal example: 500k+ daily Kathmandu commuters; average 3 rides/day; willingness to pay 10–15% premium for reliability.
  4. Validate — build a minimum test (landing page, demo, concierge MVP). Nepal example: launch a WhatsApp-based ride-booking pilot for 50 users; measure repeat rate and NPS before building the app.

(208 words)

#2.3 Target market definition (A4)

A target market is the specific segment of users you design for, message to, and sell to first — defined by demographics, geography, behaviour, and need.

#A4 · "What do you mean by target market?" [2]

A target market is the specific user segment you design for, message to, and sell to first — defined by demographics (age, income, occupation), geography (Kathmandu Valley, Tier-2 cities), behaviour (frequency, channel preference), and need (the problem you solve). Example: for a ride-sharing app, "Kathmandu professionals aged 25–40 who commute daily, value safety over price, and pay digitally."

(54 words. Definition + four segmentation bases + concrete example.)

#2.4 Evaluating business ideas

Not every idea is worth pursuing. Use a filter to decide.

#Quick evaluation framework (three filters)

Filter Question Pass =
Desirability Do users need this urgently? validated need (B12 step 4)
Feasibility Can we build/deliver it with our resources? tech stack, team, capital, timeline
Viability Can it make money sustainably? unit economics (LTV > CAC), path to scale

For the exam: if asked to "evaluate an idea," name the three filters and apply them in one sentence each.

#2.5 Prototyping development

Prototype type Fidelity Purpose Nepal example
Paper / wireframe low test flows, UI concepts sketch ride-booking flow on paper
Clickable mockup medium test usability, get feedback Figma prototype for driver app
Concierge MVP manual backend validate demand before code WhatsApp group for manual ride matching
Functional MVP working core test retention, unit economics basic app with booking + payment only

Key principle: start with the lowest fidelity that answers your riskiest assumption.

#2.6 Current technology trend analysis (B14)

Trend analysis in idea generation means scanning technology, market, and social trends — then asking "what new problems or solutions does this create?"

#B14 · "Discuss the roles of trend analysis in idea generation." [5]

Shape: three roles + Nepal example each. ~200 words.

Trend analysis plays three roles in idea generation:

  1. Opportunity spotting — a rising trend creates new needs. Example: AI/ML trend → Nepali startups building document automation for banks (KYC, loan processing) and government (licence processing).
  2. Timing validation — entering too early = no infrastructure; too late = saturated. Example: ride-sharing in 2018 (Pathao/Tootle) hit smartphone penetration + digital payments readiness; 2015 would have failed.
  3. Differentiation — trend + contrarian angle = unique positioning. Example: while others built B2C food delivery, a startup built B2B cloud kitchen management (SaaS for restaurants) — same trend (digital food), different slice.

(204 words)

#2.7 Competitor analysis (B13)

Competitor analysis is the systematic mapping of who else solves the same problem — their strengths, weaknesses, positioning, and your defensible wedge.

#B13 · "Write a short note on competitor analysis." [5]

Shape: why it matters → framework (4 quadrants) → Nepal example. ~200 words.

Competitor analysis maps who else solves your user's problem so you find a defensible wedge. Use a four-quadrant framework:

Quadrant What to map
Direct competitors same problem, same solution (Pathao vs Tootle vs inDrive)
Indirect competitors same problem, different solution (microbuses, taxis, own bike)
Substitutes different problem, same budget (walking, company shuttle)
Potential entrants adjacent players who could pivot (food delivery apps adding rides)

For each competitor, track: pricing, USPs, user reviews (Play Store/App Store), funding, partnerships, tech stack.

Nepal example: Pathao (first mover, super-app, deep funding), Tootle (motorcycle focus, community-driven), inDrive (price negotiation model, global backing). A new entrant's wedge could be safety-first for women riders (verified female drivers, SOS button, ride-sharing with contacts) — underserved by all three.

(208 words)

#2.8 Consumer behaviour insight

Insight What it means Nepal application
Price sensitivity high for students, low for professionals tiered pricing: economy/business
Trust signals ratings, verification, brand, word-of-mouth driver photos, SOS, insurance badge
Convenience > features one-tap booking beats feature-rich complex UI simple flow: open → book → ride
Network effects more riders → more drivers → shorter wait referral bonuses, launch density
Payment preference cash still dominant; digital growing wallet + cash option mandatory

#2.9 Case sub-parts (D22a, D22b)

#D22(a) · "Explain the steps you will follow for idea generation." [5]

Shape: 4–5 steps, one sentence each, with Pathao context. ~150 words.

As promoting manager for a Pathao-like ride-sharing app:

  1. Trend scan — identify rising trends: smartphone penetration, digital payments, urban congestion, gig economy.
  2. Problem observation — observe commuter pain: unsafe microbuses, unreliable taxis, no price transparency, cash-only.
  3. Technique application — run SCAMPER on "taxi service" (Substitute app for phone, Combine ride+payment, Adapt driver-partner model).
  4. MVP definition — define the riskiest assumption (will riders trust an app?) and build a concierge MVP (WhatsApp booking).
  5. Validation loop — measure repeat rate, NPS, driver earnings; iterate before scaling.

(156 words)

#D22(b) · "How do you analyze the market?" [5]

Shape: TAM/SAM/SOM + competitor map + consumer insight. ~150 words.

Market analysis for a Kathmandu ride-sharing app:

  1. TAM/SAM/SOM — Total Addressable Market: 500k+ daily commuters. Serviceable Available Market: 200k smartphone users with digital payment. Serviceable Obtainable Market: 20k riders in Year 1 (2% of SAM).
  2. Competitor map — Direct: Pathao (super-app, deep funding), Tootle (bike focus), inDrive (price negotiation). Indirect: microbuses, taxis. Wedge: safety-first for women (verified female drivers, SOS, ride-tracking).
  3. Consumer insight — Price-sensitive students vs safety-focused professionals. Trust signals: driver photo, SOS button, insurance, fare transparency. Payment: wallet + cash mandatory.
  4. Regulatory scan — Company registration (Pvt Ltd), transport permit (DoTM), labour law (driver contracts), data privacy (Privacy Act 2075), tax (VAT, TDS).

(168 words)

#2.11 Traps

Trap Why it costs marks Fix
Writing "brainstorming, mind mapping" without how/when A3 asks "list" but 2 marks = ~55 words name + one-line how-it-works + when-to-use
Defining target market as "people who buy" misses segmentation bases demographics, geography, behaviour, need — all four
B12 as a list without Nepal examples paper rewards local context one Nepal example per step
Competitor analysis as only "Pathao vs Tootle" misses indirect/substitutes/entrants four quadrants
Trend analysis as "AI is trending" misses the three roles opportunity spotting, timing validation, differentiation
Case answers without frameworks D22a/b are 5 marks each — need structure idea generation: 5 steps; market: TAM/SAM/SOM + competitors + insight + regulatory

#2.12 Self-test (answers collapsed)

  1. Name four creative thinking techniques. (2 marks — A3)
  2. Define target market with four segmentation bases. (2 marks — A4)
  3. What are the four steps to identify market needs? (3 marks)
  4. What are the three filters for evaluating a business idea? (2 marks)
  5. Name the four quadrants of competitor analysis. (3 marks — B13)
  6. What are the three roles of trend analysis in idea generation? (5 marks — B14)
  7. For a ride-sharing app, give the TAM/SAM/SOM and one wedge. (5 marks — D22b)
Answers
  1. Brainstorming, SCAMPER, Mind Mapping, Trend Analysis.
  2. Specific user segment you design/sell to first — demographics, geography, behaviour, need.
  3. Observe (context, workarounds), Interview (open-ended on problems), Quantify (size, frequency, willingness to pay), Validate (MVP, pre-sell).
  4. Desirability (validated need), Feasibility (can we build), Viability (unit economics, LTV > CAC).
  5. Direct (same problem/solution), Indirect (same problem/different solution), Substitutes (different problem/same budget), Potential entrants (adjacent players who could pivot).
  6. (1) Opportunity spotting. (2) Timing validation. (3) Differentiation.
  7. TAM: 500k+ daily commuters. SAM: 200k smartphone + digital payment. SOM: 20k Year 1. Wedge: safety-first for women (verified female drivers, SOS, tracking).

#2.13 Sixty-second check

Close the file and, on a blank page:

  • Two creative techniques: name + how + when
  • Target market: definition + 4 segmentation bases + example
  • Market needs: 4 steps (Observe, Interview, Quantify, Validate)
  • Three evaluation filters: Desirability, Feasibility, Viability
  • Competitor analysis: 4 quadrants + Nepal wedge
  • Trend analysis: 3 roles + Nepal examples
  • D22a: 5 idea generation steps
  • D22b: TAM/SAM/SOM + competitors + insight + regulatory

If all eight are there, Unit 2's 29 marks are covered — A3, A4, B12, B13, B14, D22a, D22b.
